summary:
Hatay Province stands under the national framework of Türkiye, where hostility toward trans people has been consolidated into state policy rather than left to social prejudice. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in one year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, including 299 detention decisions — 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record — alongside systematic intrusion into the privacy of LGBT people. Nothing in the sourced material distinguishes Hatay from this national pattern, and no Hatay-specific incident is documented in the inventory.

A leaked omnibus draft known as the 11th Judicial Package, reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025, would amend the penal and civil codes to criminalise LGBT conduct deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' with up to 3 years' imprisonment, criminalise same-sex ceremonies with up to 4 years, raise eligibility for gender-affirming healthcare from 18 to 25 with mandatory infertility and repeated-evaluation conditions, and expose providers to fines and up to 7 years and patients to up to 3 years. Fifteen LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association objected. Amnesty International records that three draft packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025, an unprecedented assault that would criminalise expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible; none was ultimately submitted to parliament.

The absence of enacted legislation has not restrained enforcement. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on streets, in shops and in cafés in Beyoğlu and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for 'General Information Gathering' (GBT) background checks before release; legal experts cited in the reporting argue such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that no fines were issued but that she was documented anyway, and that the new law had not passed even as it was already being applied to her. Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints must produce original identity documents, which creates a direct outing risk wherever appearance does not match the passport gender marker.

Türkiye requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira and formal warnings of detention for non-compliance. Every checkpoint interaction is therefore an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Violence against trans people is lethal and the state response asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, with transgender people disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, a detention asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Pride events are suppressed as a matter of routine. In June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful force, more than 90 people were arbitrarily detained, and prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches were still continuing at year's end. Governors have extended bans to LGBTI-focused events generally since October 2018; police dispersed the 2015 and 2016 Istanbul parades with water cannon and tear gas, and on 14 June 2019 the Istanbul, İzmir and Antalya prides were all banned. In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association, ruling that it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values' that could 'encourage or promote' LGBTI identities. Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia.

The Erdoğan government frames its position as protecting 'the family' and 'public morals', language Human Rights Watch identifies as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma. A February 2026 press report stated the government was considering a law criminalising publicly encouraging 'behavior contrary to biological sex' with one to three years' imprisonment; that measure was not included in the 12th judicial package.

Legal recognition is partial and unprotected. Homosexuality has not been a criminal offence since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988, but there is no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and same-sex marriage is not recognised. Openly LGBTQ people are barred from military service: conscripts who declare homosexuality are classified under a definition of homosexuality as a 'psychosexual illness', must provide photographic proof, and risk their 'unfit report' leaking publicly.

Trans prisoners are held according to registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Coordinated by Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın, rights groups demanded an independent investigation; accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered two days later, and that witness statements were not taken. The case, raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025, confirmed that a trans man had been held in a women's prison and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025. The Prison Insider country profile, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted healthcare access, refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners, no policy or staff training to identify LGBT prisoners' needs, binary and heteronormative administration, transfers that disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints mechanisms that are ineffective and can attract further violence.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added 'gender reassignment' as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the 'other' option and required e-reports to be issued, risking profiling of trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care.
tangentialFactors:
The depth of the regime predates the current government. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people; it predates the legal changes made after 2018 and stands as historical evidence of the pattern's duration rather than a statement of current law.

Türkiye's position differs from outright criminalisation of consensual same-sex conduct, which has not applied since 1858, and from states where legal gender recognition is unavailable, which Türkiye has permitted since 1988. The pressure is exerted instead through administrative bans, policing practice, draft legislation that shapes conduct before passage, and institutional records — a pattern in which documentation itself becomes the exposure mechanism.

Regional comparison is limited by the inventory: the sourced material covers Türkiye nationally, with Istanbul, İzmir and Antalya as the documented flashpoints for pride bans and Ankara as the site of the prison death. No neighbouring jurisdiction's treatment of trans visitors is recorded here.
localsOnly:
Residents face the same draft exposure as visitors plus obligations that fall only on them: military service classification of declared homosexuality as a 'psychosexual illness', with photographic proof required and the risk that an 'unfit report' leaks publicly.

Legal gender change has been available since 1988, but the September 2025 Health Ministry regulation and the Kayseri circular constrain the medical pathway by removing the 'other' option from records and mandating e-reports, while the draft 11th Judicial Package would raise care eligibility to 25 with infertility conditions.

There is no comprehensive statutory protection against discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity grounds, and same-sex marriage is not recognised, so redress for residents relies on litigation and advocacy rather than a discrimination claim.

Participation in public LGBTI organising carries direct legal risk: 92 prosecutions for pride participation were live at the end of 2025, and the Young LGBTI+ Association was dissolved by court order in December 2025 on 'obscene images' and 'moral values' grounds.

Detainees and prisoners face segregation by registered sex, strip searches, isolation and ineffective complaints mechanisms, with no staff training to identify LGBT needs.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Hatay-specific incident, arrest, facility rule or local enforcement practice is sourced in this inventory; the province-level record is derived entirely from national material and should be read as such.

Whether the 11th Judicial Package or any of the three draft packages reported during 2025 has since been enacted is unresolved here. The inventory records them as published drafts not submitted to parliament as of the reporting dates, and the February 2026 press report on criminalising public encouragement as considered but excluded from the 12th judicial package.

The current status of the 92 pride prosecutions and of the appeal, if any, against the İzmir court's dissolution order is not sourced.

Whether foreign visitors have been subjected to GBT-style stops in Hatay, and whether local police checkpoints in the province apply the same document-comparison practice documented in Istanbul, is not sourced and remains unverified.

The outcome of the demanded independent investigation into Poyraz's death, and of the parliamentary scrutiny raised on 12 December 2025, is unresolved in this inventory.
